title: Measures to maximise impact - Dissemination, exploitation and communication
content:
## B.2.2 Measures to maximise impact - Dissemination, exploitation and communication

The project treats dissemination, exploitation and communication as one planned function, not three closing activities. One work package, "Policy uptake, sectoral mainstreaming and exploitation" (WP7), carries them. The outline below satisfies the admissibility condition for a plan for the dissemination and exploitation of results, including communication. A more detailed plan follows as a mandatory project deliverable, updated periodically, and consolidated in the "Dissemination, exploitation and communication plan" (D7.4). Planning runs continuously from early in the project rather than at the end. The "Data management plan and shared metadata profile" (D1.1), due at month 6, fixes the open-data and FAIR commitments every dissemination measure rests on.

### Target groups and the measure matched to each

Each measure is chosen for the group it must reach. The reason it suits that group sits in the cell.

| Target group | Primary measure | Why this measure suits the group |
|---|---|---|
| Scientific community: ecosystem-assessment and biodiversity machine-learning research groups | FAIR release of the training resource, benchmarks, protocols, crosswalks and pipeline to the open science cloud and the common data spaces | Researchers reuse data and code they can find and run without asking the consortium, so open release reaches them at the lowest cost |
| Biodiversity data-infrastructure operators and the standards bodies maintaining the European habitat classification and the global ecosystem typology | Submission of the harmonisation decisions and the crosswalks, with each decision's disposition recorded | These bodies adopt a decision through their own process, so the project submits to them rather than publishing past them |
| Competent authorities under the Habitats Directive, the Birds Directive, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation | Outputs shaped to reporting obligations, starting from the "Policy reporting needs assessment" (D7.1) | An authority can use evidence only in the form its obligations take, so the assessment runs before the outputs are designed |
| End users: farmers, land and sea managers, and the agricultural holdings in the user network | Indicators delivered inside farm-management tools, with a usability evaluation | An indicator changes a decision only when it reaches the tool a practitioner already uses, so the measure places it there and asks whether they can act on it |
| The international biodiversity assessment community | Occurrence records and crosswalked labels published to the global data facilities | Evidence counts in an international assessment only when it is countable there, which a crosswalk and a global facility supply |
| Policymakers and the public at large | Plain-language evidence on the land-to-coast pressure pathway | This group needs the finding, not the dataset, so the message is the pathway rather than the data |

The form lists financial actors as a fourth target group. The project does not claim a direct measure for them. It improves the evidence a valuation of ecosystem services would rest on, but it runs no valuation, because no partner carries environmental economics. The valuation clause of the fourth destination impact is therefore only partly addressed. The project states this rather than asserting a financial-actor pathway it cannot run.

### Dissemination

Dissemination releases the results for reuse. The measures are open publication under FAIR terms, proportionate to a Research and Innovation Action of EUR 5,000,000 funding two projects. Open release is the main channel, because its marginal cost is low and its reach does not depend on an events budget.

- The "Joint data collection, metadata and processing protocols" (D3.1), the "Interoperability crosswalk package" (D3.2) and the "Provenance-tracked processing pipeline release" (D3.3) are released so an external group can rerun the chain.
- The "Documented training and validation resource with split protocol" (D6.1) and the "Habitat and ecosystem classification models and benchmarks" (D6.2) let others reproduce and extend the benchmarks.
- The "European-scale maps and biodiversity trend predictions" (D6.3) and the "Genome-to-space linkage report" (D5.3) carry the integrated results to the assessment community.
- Datasets and services are registered in the open science cloud and the common data spaces, reported in the "FAIR publication and standards contribution report" (D3.4).
- Occurrence records reach the global biodiversity data facilities through the cooperation held in WP1 and WP3.

### Exploitation

Exploitation turns the results into use by the sectors that create the pressure and the authorities that report on it. This is a Research and Innovation Action, not an Innovation Action, so the plan sets out use and uptake rather than a path to commercialise a single innovation.

- The "Biodiversity indicator decision-support release" (D7.2) and the "Farm-management integration and usability evaluation" (D7.3) carry indicators into the tools agricultural holdings already use. The uptake channel is P05's multi-country user network, a partner whose participation is assumed.
- A measurement protocol transfers to a second production context, which tests whether the method is exploitable beyond the case that designed it. This measure rests on P06, whose participation is assumed.
- The harmonisation decisions are exploited as a contribution to the bodies that maintain the classifications, not kept as an internal convention.

### Standardisation

Standardisation is a named exploitation route here. The project submits its harmonisation decisions to the bodies maintaining the European habitat classification and the global ecosystem typology. Each decision's disposition is recorded in the "FAIR publication and standards contribution report" (D3.4). The scope asks the project to contribute to consensus on joint definitions, which an internal protocol does not do. The crosswalk, open-science-cloud and standards-submission measures are held by P10, whose participation is assumed.

### Exploitation in the Union's interest

The beneficiaries sit in Member States and Associated Countries, under the consortium's assumed country-slot assignment. Exploitation is therefore not primarily in non-associated third countries. The justification the form asks for in that case does not apply here.

### Communication

Communication explains what the project finds and why it matters, to audiences that will not read the datasets. It runs across the project rather than as a closing phase, in the stakeholder and planning task of WP7. Each message travels through a channel the project already controls rather than a generic broadcast.

- To researchers and data-infrastructure operators, the message is that one reconciliation is published and reusable. The channels are the FAIR release and the standards submission.
- To competent authorities, the message is that the evidence fits their reporting obligations. The channel is the co-designed reporting-needs assessment.
- To practitioners, the message is that a biodiversity indicator can sit inside a farm-management tool. The channel is the user network.
- To policymakers and the public, the message is that agricultural pressure is now observable from land to coast. The channel is plain-language evidence, distinct from the reporting outputs.

The detailed communication measures, their tools and their quantified reach are fixed at grant preparation. No target numbers are set yet, because a target is a consortium commitment and no partner's participation is confirmed.

### Management of intellectual property

The intellectual-property strategy follows from what the project produces. Its results are protocols, crosswalks, datasets, models and software, not devices. The primary protection measure is copyright under open licences, which serves exploitation rather than restricting it.

- Software, including the pipeline release, the classification models and the decision-support release, is released under open-source licences.
- Datasets, the crosswalk package and the training resource are published under open, FAIR terms.
- Patents and design rights are not the primary route, because the outputs are not patentable devices.
- Where an SME sustains the decision-support beyond the project, its background tooling may remain a trade secret while the project's foreground results stay open. This rests on P04 and P05, partners whose participation is assumed.

Open foreground is what makes the results available and used, which is the second destination impact. Background trade secrets let an SME build a sustainable service on top of the open results. The detailed access rights belong in the consortium agreement, which is not yet drafted.

### Policy feedback

The project generates policy feedback by improving the evidence base that biodiversity policy is monitored and reviewed against. It does not design policy itself.

- Outputs are shaped to the reporting obligations under the Habitats Directive, the Birds Directive, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, starting from the "Policy reporting needs assessment" (D7.1).
- The "Interoperability crosswalk package" (D3.2) makes each habitat label resolvable against the classifications these obligations use, so project evidence enters monitoring and review without rework.
- Occurrence records and crosswalked labels make progress on international biodiversity commitments countable, which is the sixth destination impact.

The feedback is to monitoring, reporting and review, not to the drafting of new instruments. The project states this boundary rather than claiming a policy-design role it does not hold.

### Follow-up after the project

The central result is a reusable observation chain, released under open terms, so use continues after the project ends and does not depend on the consortium staying together. The project measures reuse through its impact indicators rather than promising it, and no target numbers are set yet. The "Final project report" (D1.3) records the measures delivered and the reuse observed.
